options.name: A final `OkHttpTransport : HttpTransport`, built by a factory taking a validated `userAgent` and an `OutboundUrlPolicy`, over an `internal` constructor that takes the guard and its relaxation, a `Dns` and an optional donor `OkHttpClient` for the fixtures
options.why: The factory is the one public way in, so no OkHttp type is in a public signature, and the fixtures reach the relaxation through the compilation association only.

options.name: A public `OkHttpClient` in a signature, as Apollo and Coil take one
options.why: No library type in a public signature; the donor client stays an `internal` constructor parameter for the fixtures.

options.name: Letting a caller's `Host`, `Connection`, `Accept-Encoding`, `User-Agent` and the other framing and hop-by-hop names through, as OkHttp 5.5.0 lets the caller's value win
options.why: Each changes the framing, the decoding, the target host, the protocol or the exchange's flow on at least one protocol, or behaves differently on HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2; a request carrying one of the twelve fails with `InvalidRequest` before anything is sent.

options.name: Refusing `Range` with the controlled headers, as the headers findings file recommends
options.why: `Range` interferes only with the transport's own `Accept-Encoding`, which the transport sets: on a hop that carries `Range` it sends `Accept-Encoding: identity`, so OkHttp neither adds `gzip` nor decodes, and a caller's range request is kept.

options.name: Admitting `Range` without `Accept-Encoding: identity`
options.why: With `Range` OkHttp sends no `Accept-Encoding` and decodes nothing, so a server's content coding would reach the caller undecoded (measured).

excerpt.heading: R3. The client
excerpt.paragraph: Each transport owns a new `Dispatcher` (with its own `ExecutorService`) and a new `ConnectionPool`, even when it is derived from a donor client; it never shares a pool or a dispatcher, so `close()` cannot stop someone else's threads. The client:

statements.text: A request carrying one of twelve transport-controlled headers fails with `InvalidRequest` before anything is sent, naming the first in request order; `Range` is admitted, and a hop that carries it is sent with `Accept-Encoding: identity`.

excerpt.heading: R4. The request side of `execute`, in order
excerpt.paragraph: `HttpFailure.Closed("transport")` when the transport is closed. · A request carrying a header the transport controls fails with `TransportFailure.InvalidRequest("header <Name> is controlled by the transport")` before anything is sent (no socket), naming the first such entry in request order, in the list's canonical spelling. The list is exactly twelve names: `User-Agent`, `Accept-Encoding`, `Host`, `Connection`, `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Keep-Alive`, `Proxy-Connection`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Upgrade`, `Expect`, compared with `HttpSyntax.equalsName`. statements.text: Each hop is one `Call` built from the hop's `Url` text, the caller's headers in order, the transport's `User-Agent` and a fresh exchange tag; a body goes with its content type as a plain `Content-Type` header, and no `okhttp3.internal` class is referenced.

excerpt.heading: R5. The hop
excerpt.paragraph: One `Call` per hop, one request per `Call`, no retry. The request is built from the hop's `Url` text (`url.toString().toHttpUrl()`, never rebuilt from parts), the method name as is, the caller's headers in order, the transport's `User-Agent`, and a fresh `HopExchanges` tag. A present body is sent as `bytes.toRequestBody(null)` with its content type as a plain `Content-Type` header (OkHttp's `MediaType` stays `null`); a body-required method without a body gets an empty body.
